## Conclusion

The project failed for three compounding reasons: a cost baseline that overran by 34 percent and consumed the contingency, an anchor-tenant leasing strategy that the post-2022 office market invalidated, and governance turnover that stalled capital decisions at the points where either problem could still have been corrected [1][3][4]. The largest single driver was the anchor strategy, because the unbuilt parcel accounts for both the missing revenue and the unrecovered cost [1][3]. The strongest opposing view within this record is that governance was the binding constraint rather than a contributing one — three directors in four years and two long quorum gaps would stall any correction, whatever the leasing plan [4] — and the evidence below does not cleanly separate the two. Each cause is examined in turn.

## Key findings

- Construction costs finished 34 percent over the original estimate, driven by utility relocation and two years of materials inflation [1].
- The streetscape and plaza phases were delivered complete; the anchor redevelopment parcel remains unbuilt and generated no revenue during the study period [1][3].
- Foot traffic in the district rose 22 percent between 2022 and 2025, and ground-floor vacancy declined from 28 percent to 19 percent over the same period [2].
- Small-business turnover in the district remained above the citywide average throughout [2].
- The project saw three executive directors in four years, and board minutes record two periods of six months or longer without a quorum on capital decisions [4].

## The strongest counterargument

The reading this report rejects is that governance, not leasing, was the decisive cause. On that account the anchor strategy was a defensible bet in 2021 — the market study flagged office-demand sensitivity but did not advise against it [3] — and what turned a bad bet into an unrecoverable one was the absence of anyone empowered to change course. Two quorum gaps of six months or more, straddling the period when the office market moved, meant no revised leasing plan could be approved even if staff had proposed one [4].

The objection is strong and the record does not decisively answer it. What would settle it is evidence of a proposed alternative that governance failed to act on; the board minutes record no such proposal, which is consistent with either story [4]. The conclusion above assigns primary weight to the leasing strategy because the cost overrun was already absorbed by the contingency before the quorum gaps began [1], leaving the unbuilt parcel as the outstanding item — but a reader who weights the governance account more heavily is not contradicted by anything in this record.

## Costs and outcomes

Construction costs finished 34 percent over the original estimate, driven by utility relocation and two years of materials inflation [1]. The project delivered its streetscape and plaza phases complete; the anchor redevelopment parcel remains unbuilt [1].

Foot traffic in the district rose 22 percent between 2022 and 2025, and ground-floor vacancy declined from 28 percent to 19 percent over the same period [2]. Small-business turnover in the district nonetheless remained above the citywide average [2].

## Leasing strategy

The plan reserved the anchor parcel for a single large commercial tenant, a strategy the market study had flagged as sensitive to office demand [3]. No anchor tenant signed, and the parcel generated no revenue during the study period [1][3].

The market study's own downside scenario contemplated subdividing the parcel for smaller tenants if no anchor materialised within 24 months [3]. That scenario was never activated.

Regional office absorption over the same window ran well below the market study's base case, and the economic development office recorded no comparable anchor lease anywhere in the city during the period [5]. The strategy's failure was therefore not specific to this parcel, which bears on how much of the outcome the project's own decisions can carry [3][5].

## Governance

The project saw three executive directors in four years, and board minutes record two periods of six months or longer without a quorum on capital decisions [4]. The second gap overlapped the window in which the subdivision fallback would have had to be triggered [3][4].

Turnover also broke the continuity the closeout review identifies as necessary for cost control: each incoming director inherited a contingency drawdown they had not authorised and a schedule they had not set [1]. The controller notes that no single officer held the project across both the overrun and the leasing decision [1].

## What the record does not establish

Two limits bound the causal account above. The first is that no document estimates what the closeout position would have been under an alternative leasing plan or a stable directorate, so the weight this report assigns to each cause is a judgement rather than a measurement [1][3]. The second is timing: the three causes overlap, and the closeout review reports them as a list rather than as a decomposition, which is why the counterargument section above cannot be settled from the record [1][4].

## Assessment

The failure traces to compounding causes: an over-optimistic cost baseline, an anchor-tenant strategy that a changing market invalidated, and governance instability that prevented timely correction of either [1][3][4]. On the record reviewed, the anchor parcel is the item that remains outstanding and the one a successor project would have to resolve first [3].
